content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a unsupervised learning method RankCSE for sentence embedding, which extends contrastive learning objective proposed in SimCSE with two additional constraints: ranking consistency and ranking distillation, in order to capture the fine-grained ranking information among the sentences. Experimental results on semantic textual similarity (STS) and transfer (TR) tasks demonstrate the better performance of RankCSE over several state-of-the-art baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- Strength
    - RankCSE extends the contrastive learning method in SimCSE with two additional constraints to capture the fine-grained ranking information among the sentences
        - ensuring ranking consistency between two representations with different dropout masks by minimizing the Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence between their top one probability distributions
        - distilling the ranking knowledge from pre-trained SimCSE teacher models into the RankCSE student models as guidance for learning ranking preserved sentence representations using the similarity score list from the teacher model as pseudo ranking labels
    - These two ranking preserved constraints proposed in RankCSE seem to be effective, and a wide range of experiments are conducted to verify RankCSE's performance advantage over the baselines. I also noticed that experimental results of RankCSE (BERT_base section in Table 2) also seem slightly better than that of another ICLR-2023 submission (Table 1 in "[Ranking-Enhanced Unsupervised Sentence Representation Learning](https://openreview.net/forum?id=g77JafrHWyy)" ).
- Weaknesses
    - There is still a lot of room for improvement in writing and organization of the paper. For example, it seems that Figure 1 is the most important figure as the illustration of RankCSE framework, but there is no mention or citation of Figure 1 anywhere in the main text, let alone a detailed explanation using each part of Figure 1.
    - Due to organization of the paper, the readability can be improved as well. The reader is left to guess and figure out by himself the meaning of the diagrams and the parts of the text that correspond to the diagrams. Section 4 and Figure 1 should be organically integrated for better explaining the RankCSE model in detail.
    - "ranking consistency" seems a plausible constraint of ensuring consistency between two representations with different dropout masks. However, why “ranking distillation” is effective might require more explanation in principle. In the beginning of this paper, it claims that contractive learning objective in SimCSE failed to capture ranking information among the sentences, but why the failed SimCSE is used as the teacher model in ranking distillation to transfer ranking knowledge into the RankCSE student model? The story line seems to be somewhat inconsistent.

content.title: Response to Reviewer vbX1
content.comment:
**Q1: Regarding the paper presentation.**

A1: Thank you for the great suggestions! We have revised Figure 1 and Section 4 accordingly to improve clarity and readability. Specifically, we supplemented legends in Figure 1 with a detailed explanation. We also provide more motivation and discussion in Section 4.

**Q2: Why SimCSE is used as the teacher in ranking distillation to transfer ranking knowledge into the RankCSE student model?**

A2: This is a great question. Although SimCSE is not targeting on learning ranking-aware representations, it still captures coarse-grained semantic ranking knowledge via contrastive learning (as shown in Appendix A.6 and Appendix A.7). Therefore, we propose to leverage the coarse-grained ranking knowledge from SimCSE via distillation and refine it with other losses to capture the fine-grained ranking information. As shown in the experiments, RankCSE with the distillation achieves stronger performance. We have supplemented more discussion in the revision to make this clearer. 

Thank you for the great comments and suggestions. We have revised the manuscript accordingly to improve the quality of our work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper points out that previous unsupervised sentence representation learning methods fail to capture the fine-grained ranking information among the sentences. Each sentence is only treated as either positive or negative, which is not consistent with real-world scenarios. In order to address this problem, the authors propose an approach called RankCSE for unsupervised sentence representation learning, which incorporates ranking consistency and ranking distillation with contrastive learning into a unified framework. Experimental results on STS and TR tasks demonstrate that RankCSE outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods. The authors also conduct a thorough ablation study and analysis to demonstrate the effectiveness of each component and justify the inner workings of the method.

Strength:

2. Complete ablation experiments to verify the effect of each component.

Weaknesses:

1. Pre-trained ranking model is introduced as the teacher model and provides a certain level of supervised information, which is unfair compared to other unsupervised sentence representation methods.

2. The method is not novel enough.

content.title: Response to Reviewer z7om
content.comment:
**Q1: Regarding introducing pre-trained ranking model as the teacher model, and might be unfair compared to other unsupervised sentence representation methods.**

A1: Thank you for raising this question. We try to make some clarification here. First, the teacher model is pre-trained via self-supervised learning without any supervision. Second, both teacher model and our model are using the same unsupervised data. Therefore, we believe it is a fair comparison since our method does not impose any supervised knowledge nor additional data.

**Q2: Regarding the novelty.**

A2: Thank you for pointing it out. We hope to reiterate some key contributions of our work.
- To the best of our knowledge, it is the first ranking preserving approach for unsupervised sentence representation, which we hope could serve as a baseline for future ranking-based unsupervised representation research.
- In terms of the technical contribution, we propose two effective ranking-aware objects to distinguish between negatives and learn fine-grained ranking aware representations.
- Our method outperforms the SOTA approaches by a large margin on both STS and transfer tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of the ranking modeling. We also conduct extensive experiments to verify the motivation of our method and analyze the design.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes an approach for self-supervised sentence representation learning. Three loses are combined that are based on contrastive learning, ranking consistency and ranking distillation. Authors show that by leveraging losses from learning to rank literature a richer signal for self supervision can be obtained leading to better results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
I found the proposed approach interesting, especially the use of learning to rank. I agree with the authors that the majority of self-supervised approaches treat all negative examples as equal and learning to rank can offer a better approach to distinguish between them. Empirical evaluation is extensive and shows gains on multiple real world datasets with a detailed ablation study.

Weaknesses:
The authors provide little analysis or intuition on how the three losses complement each other. For example, the consistency loss imposes stricter requirements on the distances than infoNCE so why is infoNCE still needed? From ablation in table 4 there is only a small drop in performance when infoNCE is removed and judging by table 6 the drop is within 1-2 standard deviations so likely due to noise. Similarly, what does the distillation loss achieve and why is it added? From 5.1, RankCSE-BERTlarge is learning from a weighted average of SimCSE-BERTbase and SimCSE-BERTlarge. So the student is actually the same size as the teacher and is learning from a representation space obtained through SimCSE, that doesn't have learning to rank consistency. I don't quite see how this is beneficial. Overall, I think since loss is the main novelty of this paper further analysis and justification is needed for each added component.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is easy to follow but contains grammatical errors, please consider revising. Empirical section is very well done with extensive evaluation or real-world data and ablation.
content.summary_of_the_review: I think the proposed approach is interesting and promising but further analysis and justification is needed for each proposed loss component.

content.title: Response to Reviewer SR3v
content.comment:
**Q1: The consistency loss imposes stricter requirements on the distances than infoNCE so why is infoNCE still needed?**

A1: Thanks for the great question. We keep the contrastive loss $L_{\rm{infoNCE}}$ mainly for two reasons.
- Although the consistency loss enforces the ranking consistency between two similarity lists, it does not explicitly distinguish the positives from negatives within each list. In other words, RankCSE with only consistency loss will preserve inaccurate rankings. As shown in Table 4, RankCSE with only consistency loss significantly under-performs SimCSE, while $L_{\rm{infoNCE}}$ together with consistency loss achieves much better results.
- $L_{\rm{infoNCE}}$ is complementary to the other two ranking losses, as it is designed to push apart the representations of different sentences for optimizing the representation space. As observed in Table 4, it is clear that the model performance decreases without $L_{\rm{infoNCE}}$, especially on TR tasks. Moreover, Table 6 demonstrates the consistent performance of RankCSE. We believe that $L_{\rm{infoNCE}}$ is effective and further improves the model performance.
\end{itemize}

**Q2: Regarding the distillation loss.**

A2: This is indeed a great question. We hope to provide some clarification here. 
- First, although SimCSE is not designed to learn fine-grained ranking preserving representations, it still captures coarse-grained semantic ranking information via contrastive learning (we have supplemented results on ranking metrics as well as case studies in Appendix A.6 and Appendix A.7 to better demonstrate this). Therefore, we propose to leverage the coarse-grained ranking knowledge from SimCSE via the distillation - the distillation loss is incorporated with the other losses in a unified framework to capture the fine-grained ranking information. 
- Second, we observe that better SimCSE teacher leads to better RankCSE performance. Therefore, we implement the distillation from multiple teachers to achieve the best performance.
- Third, as shown in Table 4, we observe that RankCSE with only distillation loss outperforms the teachers on STS. The reason is that RankCSE is able to preserve ranking knowledge from multiple teachers, and generalize fine-grained ranking information from multiple coarse-grained representations.

Thank you for the great questions. We have thoroughly revised the paper by incorporating the above discussion to Section 1, 4.4 and 5.3. We have also supplemented additional experimental results in the Appendix. We hope our response addresses your concerns.

content.title: General Response
content.comment:
We sincerely thank all reviewers for their valuable and helpful feedback. We revised the manuscript during the rebuttal period, and updated the revised version, which could be summarized below:
- We revised Section 1 and Section 4.4 to better explain why SimCSE is used as the teacher in ranking distillation.
- We supplemented several legends in Figure 1 with a detailed explanation and established its connection with Section 4 for better clarification.
- We supplemented the results of RankCSE with only $L_{\rm consistency}$ in Table 4 to demonstrate that RankCSE with only $L_{\rm consistency}$ will preserve inaccurate rankings.
- We supplemented more analysis and discussion on each loss function in Section 5.3 "Ablation Study".
- We supplemented results on ranking metrics as well as case studies in Appendix A.6 and Appendix A.7 to demonstrate that SimCSE still captures coarse-grained semantic ranking information via contrastive learning, while RankCSE captures fine-grained semantic ranking information.
- We fixed several grammatical errors and typos and simplified Section 5.1 considering the page limitation.
